title: People Surprised by Feedback Aren't Yet Ready to Hear Suggestions for Improvement
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that when feedback genuinely surprises someone, a leader should never deliver the diagnosis and the remedy in the same conversation. A person caught off guard needs time to push back, test the evidence, and work out how they missed the problem, and advice delivered in that moment lands on a mind that is still defending itself. The piece prescribes two conversations. The first has a single job: helping the person see what others see by sharing evidence, answering questions, and letting them argue with it, without rushing. The second opens by asking what the person has concluded since, listening for ownership in their own words, and only then moving to suggestions, where the person often brings ideas of their own. The pause between the conversations is presented as the time feedback needs to become insight, and as a requirement for lasting change.
points: Surprising feedback triggers an instinct to question whether it is true, so leaders who add recommendations in the same conversation usually miss the mark.
The first conversation should have one job: helping the person see what others see through evidence, questions, and room to argue.
Until the person has accepted the feedback, their attention stays on the past, and advice about the future cannot be absorbed.
The second conversation should start with what the person has concluded since, and the leader should listen for ownership in their own words before steering toward action.
The gap between conversations is productive time, because lasting change depends on feedback becoming the person's own insight.
quotes: Leaders who then jump to recommendations or suggestions for improvement in the same conversation usually miss the mark.
Good leaders don’t combine surprising feedback and remedy in the same conversation. They separate them into two conversations.
The first conversation has one job, which is to help the person see what others see. The leader shares the evidence, answers questions, and lets the person argue with it.
Until people come to terms with what they heard, their attention stays on the past and not the future. Advice about what to do lands on a mind that is still defending itself.
Wise leaders open by asking what the person has concluded since their first conversation, and they listen for ownership of the feedback.
The pause between the two conversations isn’t lost time. It is the time feedback needs to become insight. Lasting change requires it.
